title: Exponentials and logarithms
hook: Say a capacitor discharging through a resistor halves its voltage every 10 seconds, falling fast and then ever more slowly. Starting from 400 V, how long until it is down to 30 V?
oneBreath: Exponential change multiplies by the same factor in every equal step, so it grows or shrinks in proportion to what is there, and the number e is the base used for change that never pauses between steps. A capacitor discharging follows that curve, at a pace set by one time constant, and a hot part cooling follows much the same curve, roughly. The logarithm undoes it by answering "what power do I need?": it turns multiplying into adding, as decibels do, finds an unknown power, turns curved laws such as y = axⁿ into straight-line graphs and gives the work an ideal gas does expanding at constant temperature.

ideas.title: Growth by multiplying
ideas.oneLine: Multiplying by the same factor each equal step, such as × 1.05 for 5% a year, gives A × bˣ, which shrinks instead when b is below 1.

ideas.title: The number e
ideas.oneLine: Growth that never pauses between steps is written eᵏᵗ, where e is a fixed number like π and k is the growth rate, worked on the eˣ key.

ideas.title: The time constant: capacitors and cooling
ideas.oneLine: A discharging capacitor follows V e^(−t/RC), its time constant RC, in seconds, setting the pace, and a hot part cooling follows much the same curve.

ideas.title: Logarithms: the power you need
ideas.oneLine: A logarithm is the power a base needs to make a number, so log 1000 = 3 because 10³ = 1000, and ln uses base e.

ideas.title: The log laws and decibels
ideas.oneLine: Logs turn multiplying into adding, log(ab) = log a + log b, straight from the laws of powers, which is why gains in decibels simply add.

ideas.title: Solving exponential equations
ideas.oneLine: To find an unknown power, get the power term alone, take logs of both sides and bring the unknown down, as in finding a capacitor's discharge time.

ideas.title: Log graphs: curved laws as straight lines
ideas.oneLine: Plotting logs of readings turns laws such as y = axⁿ into straight lines, so the gradient gives an unknown power, such as n in pVⁿ = C.

ideas.title: Isothermal work: when n = 1
ideas.oneLine: An ideal gas expanding at constant temperature, pV = C, does work W = p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁), the case the power rule for integrating cannot reach.

calibration.q: A pump's value drops by 20% every year. After 5 years, roughly how much of its first value is left?
calibration.why: Each year takes 20% of what is left, not of the first value, so it keeps 0.8 each year: 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 is about 0.33. "None" takes 20% of the first value five times over.

calibration.q: A mug of tea at 80 °C, in a room at 20 °C, cools to 50 °C in 10 minutes. About how warm is it 10 minutes later?
calibration.why: Its gap to the room halves in each 10 minutes: 60 degrees, then 30, then 15, so 20 + 15 = 35 °C. 20 °C assumes it keeps losing 30 degrees, and 25 °C halves the temperature, not the gap to the room.
